despair. But if we realize that our highest and truest life
consists in this inner treasure of spiritual life, then in all our
darkness we have a light, in all the agony of our time we
have a solid ground of hope. Do we wish with all our hearts
to belong to this world of the spirit and of grace?
A period of history in which the spirit has been despised
and the word of God's grace reviled lies behind us. The world
of the spirit has once more gained an opportunity of ex-
pansion, and the word of God's grace may be freely pro-
claimed. And even now we occasionally have the shaming
experience of hearing people complain, in face of the suffer-
ings which we are still undergoing and must undergo for
some time to come, that we were better off in the days of the
old régime and should be better off now if it were still in
force. We meet people who would be ready to exchange the
intellectual freedom which has been restored to us, the
freedom from falsehood and infamy, for material well-being.
This attitude is surely the lowest stage to which a man can
sink. No! "Man shall not live by bread alone but by every
word that proceeds from the mouth of God" (Matt. 4: 4).
But the truth is that distress and want have hit people so
hard that we understand when they despair, and we do not
wish to condemn them harshly. And our challenge: do we
wish to live in the world of the spirit?—might well be put as
follows: are we able to live in that world? Is not the life of
so many of our people who have lost all their possessions and
their loved ones, but a hollow worthless shell? Are not all
their thoughts and abilities so fully claimed and absorbed
by the effort to secure the barest necessities of life that no
time or power is left them to live in the world of the spirit?
Are we not threateningly faced by the coming winter which
will surely bring us cold and hunger?
The essential answer to these questions is that in order to
live the interior life of the spirit no special time or ability is
